quiz.title: Chapter 9 Quiz: Narrowing and Closing Out
quiz.intro: Ten questions on precision connectors, translating a question into a search, and documenting that you are done.

options: the two terms appear within five words of each other in either order
both terms appear anywhere in the document
items.why: /n is a proximity connector; pre/n adds order; ATLEAST adds frequency (The Full Connector Set).

options: Returns only documents that discuss preemption substantively, at least three times, rather than in passing
items.why: Frequency connectors find documents where a concept is a major focus (The Full Connector Set).

items.q: The chapter says a well-drafted research question is:
options: In effect a Boolean search waiting to be formatted: key terms become search terms and their relationships become connectors
items.why: This is the most direct link between the method and the mechanics (Translating Your Research Question into a Precision Search).

items.q: What is wrong with ADA AND accommodation AND remote AND anxiety for the remote-work question?
options: Every concept is welded to a single word (so telecommuting cases vanish) and nothing requires the concepts to appear near each other
It lacks a jurisdiction filter only
It is too narrow because of proximity connectors
items.why: Gather synonyms with OR, require co-occurrence with AND, and use proximity for the relationship that matters (The Bad Translation).

items.q: Westlaw, Lexis+, and Bloomberg Law connector syntax is:
options: Similar but not identical (e.g., Bloomberg uses W/n), and a misread connector can silently exclude the authority you need
items.why: Check the database’s documentation before you trust a precision search (Database-Specific Connector Syntax; Common Pitfalls).

options: Each search string, the database, the number of results, and whether the search was productive
Only the cases you plan to cite
items.why: It works alongside the Research Log and supports your closure documentation (Building a Search Log).

items.q: The closing-out protocol’s final sweep requires at least one search with different terms and at least one search aimed at:
options: The same terms in another database
Authority that cuts against your position
items.why: Even when it turns up nothing new, that search creates a documented record and answers to Rule 3.3 (The Closing-Out Protocol).

options: Cases via a citator, statutes for pending amendments and session laws, and regulations via the eCFR date and the LSA
Only authorities you plan to quote
items.why: The next step, Confirm your propositions, then has you read each authority for the specific proposition you cite it for (The Closing-Out Protocol).

items.q: A search returns no results. The chapter says this means:
options: Either there is no authority or your search was too narrow, and only after exhausting alternatives is a “no law” conclusion defensible
items.why: “I could not find it” and “it does not exist” are very different claims (The Difference Between No Results and No Law).

options: Because it protects you professionally: you can show exactly what you searched and why you concluded it was enough
Because the client reads the log
items.why: The protocol’s last step names the kind of closure, analytical or practical, and records what you searched and why you stopped (The Closing-Out Protocol; Chapter Recap).
